title: Miracle-working faith is a special gift; justifying faith is named; Rome confuses it with historical faith

pass_b_english: But there is also a certain faith which is counted among the peculiar gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:9), and which does not fall to all who are in the Church, but to a few, as it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit. This is the faith through which miracles are wrought, from which it has also received its name. And it is found in the one who, called by God to work miracles and having a promise concerning this matter — as the Apostles had from the mouth of Christ, and many others from an inward revelation of the Spirit — does not hesitate or distrust, but is certainly persuaded that God is able and willing to accomplish those stupendous works through him. Of this faith Christ speaks in Mark 11:22 when he says to the disciples, Have faith in God. Amen I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, Be taken up and cast into the sea, and does not doubt in his heart but believes that what he says will happen, it will be done for him, whatever he says (Mark 11:22-23). He also reproaches the disciples for the defect of this faith in Matthew 17:20, when he refers the cause why they could not cast out the demon to their unbelief. And to this the Apostle looks in 1 Corinthians 13:2: If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.

Finally there is another faith, to which Scripture attributes our righteousness and salvation, to which it urgently and often exhorts us, and which it adorns with the highest praises and elogies. And this is the faith which we name justifying, saving, living, and true.

But here we have a dispute with the Doctors of the Roman Church: for they confuse justifying faith with that which we have just called historical, and put no distinction between them, but want them to be plainly one and the same. Then they also teach that the faith of miracles is nothing other than a certain excellent grade of justifying faith.
source_text:
VIII. Sed et est quaedam fides, quae inter peculiaria Spiritus dona recensetur 1 Cor. 12. 9. quaeque non omnibus, qui sunt in Ecclesia, obtingit: sed paucis quibusdam; prout visum est Spiritui Sancto. Haec est fides, per quam miracula eduntur, unde quoque nomen est sortita. Atque in ea reperitur, qui a Deo vocatus ad edenda miracula, et super hac re promissionem habens, quemadmodum Apostoli habuerunt ex ore Christi, et multi alii ex interna Spiritus revelatione, non haesitat, nec diffidit: sed certo persuasus est Deum posse et velle stupenda illa opera per ipsum efficere. De hac fide loquitur Christus Marc. 11. 22. dum discipulis ait, Habete fidem Dei. Amen dico vobis, quicunque dixerit huic monti, Tollitor, et projicitor in mare, nec dubitaverit in corde suo, sed crediderit futura quae dicit, fiet ei quicquid dixerit. Hujus quoque fidei defectum, discipulis exprobrat Matt. 17. 20. dum refert in eorum incredulitatem causam, cur non potuissent daemonem ejicere. Et ad hanc respicit Apostolus, 1 Cor. 13. Si habeam, inquit, omnem fidem, ita ut montes transferam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum.

IX. Denique est alia fides, cui Scriptura justitiam et salutem nostram tribuit, ad quam nos vehementer et frequenter hortatur, quamque summis laudibus et elogiis ornat. Et haec est, quam justificantem, salutarem, vivam, veramque nuncupamus.

X. Hic autem nobis est lis cum Doctoribus Ecclesiae Romanae: confundunt enim illi fidem justificantem cum illa quam modo historicam diximus, nullamque inter eas distinctionem ponunt: sed volunt plane unam et eandem esse. Tum etiam docent fidem miraculorum, nihil esse aliud quam excellentem quendam gradum fidei justificantis.
